shots.title: Saturated
shots.engineer: Here is a typical web application with one database. Every page view reads from it: product lists, profiles, search results. Only a small share of the traffic writes anything. Say ten thousand queries a second, nine in ten of them reads. The database's CPU and disk are saturated, queries queue, and the few writes that matter, like orders, wait behind thousands of reads. These numbers are illustrative, but the shape is common: the bottleneck is reading, not writing.
shots.executive: One database answers every request, most of them reads, and it has run out of capacity.

shots.title: Scale up
shots.engineer: The obvious fix is a bigger machine. Move to the largest instance you can buy, with more cores, more memory and faster disks. It works for a while, and it needs no code changes. But each step up costs more than the last, and eventually there is no bigger machine to buy. Worse, it is still one machine: when it fails, or is restarted for maintenance, every read and every write stops together. Scaling up buys time, not a design.
shots.executive: A bigger database server helps for a while, but there is a largest size, and it is still a single point of failure.

shots.title: Parts
shots.engineer: Read replicas. Keep one primary database that accepts every write. Every change it makes is already recorded in its log: the write-ahead log in PostgreSQL, the binary log in MySQL. Stream that log to one or more replicas, which replay it and so hold copies of the same data. Replicas accept read-only queries. A router, in the application, the driver or a proxy, sends writes to the primary and reads to the replicas. Add replicas, and read capacity grows with them.
shots.executive: One main database takes all the changes and copies them to read-only copies, which share the work of answering reads.

shots.title: Write then read
shots.engineer: Step by step. The application updates a price. The router sends the write to the primary, which commits it and records it in its log. With asynchronous replication, the default in both PostgreSQL and MySQL, the primary answers straight away, without waiting for any replica. Separately, it streams the log record to each replica, which replays it. PostgreSQL's documentation says this delay is typically under one second. A moment later, a read goes to a replica and sees the new price.
shots.executive: Changes are saved on the main database first and copied to the replicas a moment later; reads then come from the copies.

shots.title: Routing
shots.engineer: Where does the split between reads and writes live? In the application, you keep two connection pools and choose per query. In the driver: PostgreSQL's libpq can list several hosts and pick one with target session attrs, such as read-write or prefer-standby. In a proxy: ProxySQL sends queries to a primary or replica host group by rules. Its own guide warns that a blanket rule sending every select to replicas causes problems with transactions and consistency. Route deliberately, not by keyword.
shots.executive: Something has to decide which database each query goes to: the application, its database driver, or a proxy in between.

shots.title: Stale read
shots.engineer: Now the catch: replicas are behind. A user changes their display name. The write commits on the primary. They reload the page, the read goes to a replica that is two seconds behind, and their old name comes back. Their edit seems to have vanished. This breaks a guarantee called read-your-writes: a process that writes something should see that write when it reads afterwards. PostgreSQL's documentation puts it plainly: data on a standby is eventually consistent with the primary.
shots.executive: Because copies lag slightly behind, a user can save a change and then not see it on the next page.

shots.title: Backwards
shots.engineer: A second surprise. The user reloads again, and this time the router picks a different replica, one further behind. Now they see something even older than before. Time appears to run backwards. The guarantee broken here is monotonic reads: once you have seen a version, later reads should not show an older one. It happens whenever one user's reads are spread across replicas with different lag, which a simple round-robin load balancer will happily do.
shots.executive: Reading from different copies in turn can even show a user older data than they saw a moment ago.

shots.title: Sticky reads
shots.engineer: The fixes. After a user writes, send their reads to the primary for a short while, longer than your usual lag; this is often called sticky reads. Or remember the log position of their write, and only read from a replica that has replayed past it. For monotonic reads, send each user to the same replica every time, for example by hashing their id. And read anything that must be exact, such as a balance before a payment, from the primary.
shots.executive: After someone saves a change, read their data from the main database for a short while, and keep each user on the same copy.

shots.title: Failover
shots.engineer: What if the primary dies? You promote a replica. In PostgreSQL that is pg_ctl promote, but PostgreSQL itself does not detect the failure; external tooling must. With asynchronous replication, commits that had not reached the replica are lost, in proportion to the lag at that moment. Then the old primary restarts. If nothing tells it that it is no longer primary, both accept writes: split brain. PostgreSQL's documentation calls the remedy STONITH: shoot the other node in the head.
shots.executive: If the main database fails, a copy takes over, but the last few changes can be lost, and the old one must be stopped from coming back as a second boss.

shots.title: Sync modes

card.heading: How long should a commit wait?
points: Asynchronous | Fastest writes; failover can lose recent commits
Semi-synchronous (MySQL) | Waits for one replica to receive and log; falls back to async after a timeout
Synchronous (PostgreSQL) | Waits for standby flush, or replay with remote_apply; slower writes
Any mode | Replicas still serve reads; only commit latency and durability change

shots.engineer: How long should a commit wait? Asynchronous: the primary does not wait, so writes are fast, but a failover can lose recent commits. Semi-synchronous, in MySQL: the commit waits until at least one replica has received and logged it, though not applied it. If no replica answers within the timeout, ten seconds by default, it falls back to asynchronous. Synchronous, in PostgreSQL: wait for the standby to flush the commit, or with remote apply, to replay it. Each wait adds latency to every write.
shots.executive: Making the main database wait for its copies protects recent changes in a failure, but slows every write.

shots.title: Limits

card.heading: What replicas do not fix
points: Writes: every replica replays every write; the primary is the ceiling
To scale writes, split the data: sharding
Cost: each replica is a full database instance
Cross-region replicas: closer reads and disaster recovery, but more lag

shots.engineer: Three limits. Replicas do not help writes. Every replica replays every write, so the primary's write capacity is the ceiling; to scale writes, split the data with sharding. Replicas cost money: Amazon RDS bills each one as a standard database instance. And replicas in another region bring reads closer to distant users and give you a copy for disaster recovery, but AWS notes their lag is higher, because the network path between regions is longer.
shots.executive: Copies spread out reading, not writing. Each one costs a full server, and copies far away lag further behind.

shots.title: Sources
shots.engineer: In the wild. PostgreSQL streams write-ahead log records to standbys, and hot standby lets them answer read-only queries. MySQL replicates from the source's binary log, asynchronous by default, with semisynchronous as an option. Amazon RDS read replicas use each engine's own asynchronous replication, can live in another region, and can be promoted to standalone. Aurora is different: up to fifteen replicas share one storage volume, so lag is usually well under a hundred milliseconds, and a replica is promoted automatically on failure.
shots.executive: PostgreSQL and MySQL have this built in, and Amazon's managed databases offer it as a setting, with Aurora sharing storage to keep copies very close.

card.heading: Related patterns
points: Cache-aside | Absorbs repeated reads before they reach any replica
Sharding | Splits the data so writes scale too; each shard can have replicas
CQRS | Builds a separate read model shaped for queries
Write-ahead log | The ordered record of changes that replicas replay

shots.engineer: Its neighbours. Cache-aside sits in front and absorbs repeated reads before they reach any replica. Sharding answers the write limit: split the data so each primary owns a slice, and each shard can still have its own replicas. CQRS goes further than copying the same tables: it builds a separate read model shaped for the queries you actually run. And the write-ahead log is the building block underneath: the ordered record of changes that every replica replays.
shots.executive: Caches, splitting data across databases, and purpose-built read models all work alongside read copies.

card.heading: Recap
points: Writes to one primary; stream its log to replicas that serve reads
Replicas lag: read your own writes from the primary; keep users on one replica
Plan failover: know what async can lose, and fence the old primary

shots.engineer: Three things to remember. Send writes to one primary and stream its log to replicas that serve reads; it scales reads, never writes. Replicas lag, so design for it: read your own writes from the primary or a caught-up replica, and keep each user on one replica. And plan failover before you need it: know what asynchronous replication can lose, and fence the old primary so it never comes back as a second one.
shots.executive: Copies scale reading, not writing. Expect them to lag. Plan carefully for the main database failing.
